title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
gist: A Zhuque-2E upper stage from LandSpace, after launching 10 Qianfan satellites on September 15, fell on a Minnesota cornfield as an 11-foot object, probably after a botched deorbit burn. The incident highlights Chinese debris practices and China's Qianfan push to rival Starlink.

insights.claim: An approximately 11-foot metal object found in a Minnesota cornfield matches the diameter of the Zhuque-2E upper stage, which launched with Qianfan satellites on September 15.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Establishes a physical, attributable link between a Chinese commercial launch and US ground debris.
insights.quote: The upper stage of the Zhuque-2E rocket has a diameter of 11 feet, or 3.35 meters, perfectly matching the size of the object found in Minnesota.

insights.claim: The unusual deorbit over the US Midwest, rather than the ocean, suggests a botched deorbit burn, and LandSpace has not publicly acknowledged it.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Reliability and transparency of Chinese commercial launchers face scrutiny.
insights.quote: suggesting the incident on September 15 was perhaps the result of a botched deorbit burn

insights.claim: Under international law the launching country is liable for ground damage caused by space objects, creating potential liability exposure for China if debris causes harm.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Debris falling over populated areas could create diplomatic and legal friction.
insights.quote: Under international law, the country that launched an object into space is liable for any damage it causes on the ground.

insights.claim: Debris this large surviving reentry is unusual, and the outcome would have been worse over a populated area, though no one has ever been seriously injured by space junk.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Large uncontrolled reentries are a tail risk as launch cadence rises.

insights.claim: Chinese rockets have repeatedly had unguided reentries and in-orbit breakups, whereas US low-orbit rockets usually reserve propellant for guided disposal.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Debris-management gaps are a competitive and regulatory weak point for China's constellations.
insights.quote: US rockets on low-Earth orbit missions usually reserve enough propellant for guided disposal.

insights.claim: The previous Zhuque-2E upper stage broke apart in June, leaving dozens of debris pieces in crowded low-Earth orbit near the ISS and a significant portion of Starlink.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Orbital debris from rival constellations raises collision risk for Starlink.

insights.claim: China has launched 258 Qianfan satellites since 2024 toward an initial 1,296-satellite constellation, with longer-term ambitions above 15,000, as a counterpart to Starlink.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: China's megaconstellation is scaling, intensifying competition with SpaceX.
insights.quote: China has launched 258 Qianfan satellites over a series of missions since 2024

insights.claim: The September 15 mission put 10 Qianfan satellites into a roughly 560-mile polar orbit from the Dongfeng commercial zone, co-located with the military-run Jiuquan launch center.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Commercial and military launch infrastructure overlap in China.
